prompt: Write a Python program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that simulates a greenhouse environment, displaying simulated temperature and humidity on two HD44780 16x2 LCDs and simulating actuator control, using the RPi.GPIO library. Initialize LCD 1 (temperature) with RS=GPIO7, E=GPIO8, D4=GPIO25, D5=GPIO24, D6=GPIO23, D7=GPIO18, and LCD 2 (humidity) with RS=GPIO16, E=GPIO20, D4=GPIO26, D5=GPIO19, D6=GPIO13, D7=GPIO6, both in 4-bit mode. Control LCD 1's backlight with PWM on GPIO12 and LCD 2's backlight with PWM on GPIO5, both at 1000 Hz. Use an enable pulse width of 0.0005 seconds and an enable delay of 0.0005 seconds for LCD timing. Simulate temperature readings between 15-40°C and humidity readings between 30-90%, updating every 5 seconds. If temperature exceeds 35°C, cool by 1°C every 2 seconds until it reaches 30°C or below; if it drops below 20°C, heat by 1°C every 2 seconds until it reaches 25°C or above. If humidity exceeds 85%, dehumidify by 2% every 2 seconds until it reaches 75% or below; if it drops below 40%, humidify by 2% every 2 seconds until it reaches 50% or above. Toggle the backlight state on both LCDs every 30 seconds, independently of the temperature and humidity simulation, and continuously adjust backlight brightness on both LCDs via PWM duty-cycle changes from 0-100% in steps of 10, every 1 second. Implement robust error handling around GPIO pin initialization, PWM channel setup for both backlights, and the LCD write sequences. Log every simulated reading, actuator action, and backlight change to greenhouse.log at INFO level, and ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including handling KeyboardInterrupt via signal handling so both PWM channels and all GPIO pins are released.

prompt: Write a Python environmental monitoring application for a Raspberry Pi that reads simulated temperature, humidity, and air-quality data every 5 seconds and displays the readings on a 128x64 SSD1306 OLED at I2C address 0x3C on bus 1, using the smbus2 library and PIL for rendering. Show a scrolling status banner at the bottom of the display, reading 'System OK' or an alert message, with a scroll interval of 0.05 seconds, rendered using the font at /usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu/DejaVuSans.ttf. Trigger an alert if temperature exceeds 30°C, falls below 18°C, humidity exceeds 70%, falls below 40%, or air quality exceeds 75. When an alert is active, pulse an LED on GPIO18 at a 500 Hz PWM frequency using the gpiozero library. Log every reading, including simulated sensor failures, to an SQLite database at environmental_data.db. Implement robust error handling for I2C, database, and GPIO initialization failures, and ensure clean shutdown of all resources on SIGINT or SIGTERM.
code: $ python3 environmental_monitor.py

prompt: Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi (any model) that reads a config.json file containing gpio_button_pin (an integer, e.g. 17) and update_interval_seconds (an integer, minimum 300, clamped to that minimum). Create a SQLite database named air_quality.db with a table readings holding columns timestamp (TEXT, ISO 8601), aqi (INTEGER), and pm25 (REAL). If gpio_button_pin is present and valid (a non-null integer from 1 to 27), initialize RPi.GPIO in GPIO.BCM mode, configure the pin as an input with a pull-up resistor (GPIO.PUD_UP), and register GPIO.FALLING edge detection with a 200ms debounce time whose callback prints a detailed explanation of AQI and its health implications. Every update_interval_seconds, simulate an air-quality reading (AQI 0-200, PM2.5 5-35) with a 20% chance of a simulated sensor error returning None; on success insert the reading into the database and simulate an e-paper display update by printing a formatted block with the timestamp, AQI, PM2.5 to two decimal places, and an alert string based on AQI: below 50 'GREEN Good', 50-99 'YELLOW Moderate', 100-149 'ORANGE Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups', and 150 or above 'RED Unhealthy'. Log all config, GPIO, database, and sensor errors with timestamps to air_quality_monitor.log, handling a missing config file and GPIO initialization failure gracefully by disabling the button and continuing. On exit, whether by KeyboardInterrupt or error, clean up the GPIO pins.
code: $ python3 air_quality_monitor.py

Handle OSError for I2C failures such as a locked bus or a device absent at 0x27. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handler so Ctrl+C closes the bus cleanly, and always call i2c_bus.close() on exit.

I2C LCD Ready

prompt: Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi that integrates YOLOv5 object detection with LED feedback and an I2C LCD system monitor. Initialize BCM GPIO pins 17, 18, 23, 27, and 22 as outputs using gpiozero LED components, mapping detected object classes to LEDs as class 0 to GPIO27, class 1 to GPIO17, class 2 to GPIO22, class 3 to GPIO18, and class 4 to GPIO23; when an object is detected, turn its corresponding LED on for 0.5 seconds then off, and handle the case where a detected class is not mapped. Initialize a 16x2 I2C LCD on bus 1 at address 0x27 using smbus2, and run a background daemon thread that updates the LCD every 1 second with CPU usage (via psutil) and CPU temperature (read from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp). Handle I2C bus initialization and LCD write errors gracefully so the monitor thread does not crash. Implement SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handling for graceful shutdown: on termination, clear the LCD, turn off its backlight, turn off all LEDs, and release GPIO resources cleanly. Integrate this into a standard YOLOv5 inference loop so that, when detection results contain bounding boxes, each one triggers the LED corresponding to its detected class.

prompt: Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi that reads temperature and humidity from a DHT22 sensor connected to GPIO4 (board.D4) and displays the values on a 128x64 I2C OLED display (SSD1306). Use the adafruit-circuitpython-dht library, imported as adafruit_dht, for the sensor, and adafruit_ssd1306 for the OLED, initializing I2C using board.SCL and board.SDA. Display temperature in Celsius and humidity as a percentage, both formatted to one decimal place, clearing the OLED before each update. Implement a retry mechanism for sensor read errors by catching RuntimeError, and maintain a 2-second delay between readings. Handle KeyboardInterrupt to exit gracefully, ensuring the OLED is cleared and I2C resources are released on termination.
code:
import board
import busio
import digitalio
import adafruit_ssd1306
import adafruit_dht
import time

# Create the I2C interface.
i2c = busio.I2C(board.SCL, board.SDA)

# Create the OLED class.
# The first two parameters are the pixel width and pixel height.  Change these
# to the right size for your display!
oled = adafruit_ssd1306.SSD1306_I2C(128, 64, i2c)

# Clear display.
oled.fill(0)
oled.show()

# Create sensor object.
sensor = adafruit_dht.DHT22(board.D4)

# Main loop.
while True:
    try:
        # Wait a few seconds between measurements.
        time.sleep(2)

        # Get sensor reading.
        temperature_c = sensor.temperature
        humidity = sensor.humidity

        # Clear display.
        oled.fill(0)
        oled.show()

        # Display temperature and humidity.
        oled.text("Temp: {:.1f}C".format(temperature_c), 0, 0)
        oled.text("Humidity: {:.1f}%".format(humidity), 0, 10)
        oled.show()

    except RuntimeError as error:
        # Clear display.
        oled.fill(0)
        oled.show()

        # Display error.
        oled.text("Retrying...", 0, 0)
        oled.show()

    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        # Clear display.
        oled.fill(0)
        oled.show()

        # Exit.
        break

prompt: Write a Python program for a Raspberry Pi Zero W that controls a Waveshare 2.13-inch e-Paper HAT (Black/White) via SPI (bus 0, chip select 0, 1 MHz) using spidev for SPI and RPi.GPIO for GPIO, with BCM pins RST_PIN=17, DC_PIN=25, and BUSY_PIN=24. Implement reset_display() to pull RST low for 10ms then high for 10ms. Implement clear_display() to send the full Waveshare initialization sequence over SPI setting a full 250x122 memory area and writing white data to all pixels, using commands 0x12 (software reset), 0x01 (driver output control), 0x11 (data entry mode), 0x44 and 0x45 (set RAM X/Y address start/end), 0x4E and 0x4F (set RAM X/Y address counter), 0x24 (write RAM), 0x50 (write VCOM register), 0x02 (power off), and 0x07 (deep sleep). Implement update_price(price) to clear the display, then render 'Price: $' followed by the price to two decimal places using a simple 8x16 bitmap font; the text rendering may be simulated by printing to the console and sending a placeholder pattern, but the code must be structured to accept real pixel data. Implement get_simulated_price() to return a random float between 1.00 and 99.99. In the main loop, initialize, reset, and clear the display, then generate a new price and update the display every 5 seconds. On KeyboardInterrupt, clear the display, power it off, close SPI, and clean up GPIO. Check SPI open success and GPIO setup, catch exceptions during SPI transactions, and use try/finally to guarantee resource cleanup.

prompt: Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi that continuously measures distance using an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor and prints the result every 1 second, using the RPi.GPIO library with GPIO.BOARD physical-pin numbering. Connect the trigger pin to physical pin 8 and the echo pin to physical pin 18. Send a 10-microsecond (0.00001s) high pulse on the trigger pin to start each measurement, and calculate distance from the echo pulse duration using a sonic speed of 34300 cm/s, with distance = (time_elapsed * 34300) / 2. Implement robust error handling: catch exceptions during GPIO setup, add timeout logic so the program does not hang if the echo pin never transitions because the sensor is absent or disconnected, and validate that each measured distance falls within the realistic range of 2 to 400 cm. Ensure proper cleanup of GPIO resources on all exit paths, including graceful handling of KeyboardInterrupt (Ctrl+C).

prompt: Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi obstacle-avoidance robot using the RPi.GPIO library in BCM numbering mode, with a front-facing HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor and an L298N motor driver. Configure trigger on GPIO17 and echo on GPIO27 for the front sensor, an LED indicator on GPIO22, and motor driver inputs IN1=GPIO16, IN2=GPIO12, IN3=GPIO21, IN4=GPIO20, initializing trigger and motor pins as outputs and echo as an input, with robust error handling for GPIO initialization. Implement a measure_distance() function for the front sensor that triggers a 10-microsecond pulse and measures the echo response, timing out after 0.05 seconds and returning infinity if no echo is received, so it never blocks. Implement motor control functions for forward, backward, left, right, and stop. Implement an obstacle-avoidance loop that takes 5 distance samples, averages the valid ones, and if the distance is less than 15 cm, stops, moves backward for 1.5 seconds, turns (alternating left and right) for 1.5 seconds, and stops for 1 second before continuing; otherwise it moves forward. Turn the LED on GPIO22 on for 5 seconds immediately after initialization, then off before entering the avoidance loop. Use a 1-second delay for short movements (stops) and a 1.5-second delay for long movements (backward and turns). Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including handling KeyboardInterrupt to stop the motors and clean up GPIO.

prompt: Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi using RPi.GPIO and time to measure distance with an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor and compute water level in a 50cm tank. Connect TRIG to GPIO17 and ECHO to GPIO18 (BCM numbering); since the HC-SR04's ECHO output is 5V, use a voltage divider or level shifter so the Pi receives 3.3V, with the sensor's VCC at 5V and GND shared with the Pi. Hold TRIG low for 200ms at startup to stabilize the sensor, then trigger a 10-microsecond high pulse on GPIO17 and measure the duration of the resulting high echo pulse on GPIO18, using a 30ms timeout while waiting for ECHO to go high and while waiting for it to return low so the program never hangs if the sensor is disconnected or faulty. Compute distance as duration * 34300 / 2 using a speed of sound of 34300 cm/s, and compute water level as 50 minus distance, clamping the displayed water level to the range 0 to 50cm. Reject distances outside the HC-SR04's valid range of 2 to 400cm as invalid, printing an error and skipping that measurement. Print the distance and water level every 2 seconds. Install a signal handler for SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown, wrap GPIO setup and each measurement loop iteration in try/except so I/O errors are reported without crashing, and always call GPIO.cleanup() on exit, including signal-triggered and exception paths. Do not use wiringPi or any deprecated APIs.

Write a Python control loop for a Raspberry Pi robot that intercepts a ball and then reaches a goal, using gpiozero for motor control with the left motor on PWM pins GPIO12/GPIO13 and the right motor on PWM pins GPIO18/GPIO19, printing telemetry to the console. Compute an image point beyond the ball on the line from the ball to the goal, at a distance of extension=50 past the ball, and compute the car's heading from its front position (180, -15) and back position (200, -15). prompt: Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi hydroponics monitoring and control system. Read water level using a VL53L0X time-of-flight sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x29, measuring distance to the water surface in millimeters, using the adafruit-circuitpython-vl53l0x library and smbus2 for I2C. Read nutrient level using an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor with trigger on GPIO23 and echo on GPIO24, measuring distance to the nutrient solution surface in centimeters, implemented as a direct GPIO-based measurement with the gpiozero library. Control a water pump on GPIO17 (active high): activate it when water_level is below 100mm and deactivate it when water_level exceeds 150mm, using hysteresis so that once on it stays on until water_level reaches 150mm or more, and once off it stays off until water_level drops below 100mm. Control a nutrient pump on GPIO27 (active high): activate it for exactly 5 seconds when nutrient_level is below 5cm, then deactivate it automatically. Print the water level in millimeters and the nutrient level in centimeters every 1 second. For each sensor read, handle errors such as a disconnected sensor, an I2C bus error, or a timeout by printing an error message and returning a sentinel value of -1 for that distance, without crashing; also handle GPIO initialization errors. Handle Ctrl+C (SIGINT) gracefully by turning off both pumps immediately and exiting cleanly, ensuring all GPIO and I2C resources are released on exit.

prompt: Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi (BCM GPIO numbering) implementing a dual-ultrasonic parking assistant with front and rear HC-SR04 sensors, using the RPi.GPIO library. Pin assignments: front trigger=GPIO17, front echo=GPIO18, front LED=GPIO22; rear trigger=GPIO23, rear echo=GPIO24, rear LED=GPIO27; plus a green LED on GPIO5 and a red LED on GPIO6. Configure the echo pins with pull-down resistors. Generate a 10-microsecond trigger pulse to start each measurement, using a 0.5-second timeout while waiting for the echo pulse to start and end. Sample at 10Hz using time.sleep, and apply a moving-average filter with a window size of 5 to smooth the distance readings. Continuously read both sensors, display the distances, and control the LEDs: the green LED is on by default, the red LED turns on if either distance is below 20cm (critical), and each sensor's individual LED turns on if its distance is below 50cm (warning). Implement robust error handling: check every GPIO setup call, handle sensor timeouts gracefully by returning None, validate distances against the 2 to 400cm range, and log errors to a file. On program exit, including KeyboardInterrupt, ensure all GPIO pins are cleaned up.

prompt: Write a Python program for a Raspberry Pi that reads distance from an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor and controls an LED based on a proximity threshold, using the gpiozero library with BCM numbering (not RPi.GPIO or wiringPi). Connect TRIG to GPIO17 (output) and ECHO to GPIO27 (input); since the HC-SR04's ECHO line is 5V logic, use a voltage divider (e.g. 1kΩ/2kΩ) so the Pi sees about 3.3V. Connect the LED anode to GPIO22 through a 330Ω resistor, with the cathode to ground. Every 0.5 seconds, trigger a 10-microsecond high pulse on TRIG, add a short settling delay, then measure the ECHO pulse width and convert it to distance using distance_cm = pulse_us / 58.0, based on sound travelling at approximately 343 m/s. If the measured distance is less than 20cm, turn the LED on; otherwise turn it off. Print the measured distance, rounded to 2 decimal places, on each cycle. Guard against ECHO never going high or never going low, using a timeout of about 30 milliseconds for each; if either timeout fires, print a warning, turn the LED off, and continue. Reject out-of-range readings below 2cm or above 400cm as invalid. Handle KeyboardInterrupt and SIGTERM gracefully, ensuring all GPIO resources are released on exit.

Send a 10-microsecond trigger pulse on GPIO23, then measure the duration of the echo pulse on GPIO24, including timeout handling (about 100 milliseconds) to prevent infinite blocking if the sensor is disconnected or the echo pin never transitions. Calculate distance in centimeters using distance = pulse_duration * 17150, and print the result rounded to two decimal places. Initialize GPIO17 and GPIO4 (BCM) as simulated input pins using gpiozero.InputDevice with pull_up=False, printing a confirmation message after successful initialization. Every 5 seconds (time.sleep(5)), simulate sensor readings: light level on GPIO17 as 600-1000 lux during daytime (06:00-18:00 local) or 100-300 lux at night; temperature on GPIO4 as 20-30°C; and voltage/current as 11.5-12.5V and 1.5-2.5A when light exceeds 300 lux, or 10.0-11.0V and 0.5-1.0A otherwise. Read the Raspberry Pi's internal temperature via vcgencmd measure_temp using subprocess.run with a timeout, parsing the temp=XX.X'C format; if vcgencmd is missing or fails, return None and log a warning without crashing. Trigger threshold actions, printed immediately after each log line: a WARNING about possible solar panel performance issues when light is below 300 lux; a WARNING with simulated cooling-system activation when the simulated temperature exceeds 35°C; and a CRITICAL warning with a simulated system shutdown when the Pi's internal temperature exceeds 75°C. Wrap each sensor simulation and the Pi temperature read in try/except, logging errors and falling back to a safe default (0 or None) on failure without crashing, and handle KeyboardInterrupt gracefully with a message. Log each cycle with a YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS timestamp, light in lux, temperature in °C, voltage in V, current in A, and Pi temperature in °C or N/A. #!/usr/bin/env python3

import json
import random
import time
import threading
import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt

# MQTT broker address and port
MQTT_BROKER = 'test.mosquitto.org'
MQTT_PORT = 1883

# Keepalive interval in seconds
KEEPALIVE = 60

# Number of messages to publish
NUM_MESSAGES = 5

# Publish topic
TOPIC = 'classroom/temperature'

# Publish payload
PAYLOAD = {
    'index': 0,
    'temperature': 0.0
}

# Publish payload helper function
def publish_payload(index, temperature):
    PAYLOAD['index'] = index
    PAYLOAD['temperature'] = temperature
    return json.dumps(PAYLOAD)

# Publish callback
def on_publish(client, userdata, mid):
    print('Published message {} to topic {}.'.format(PAYLOAD['index'], TOPIC))

# Connect callback
def on_connect(client, userdata, flags, rc):
    print('Connected to broker {} on port {}.'.format(MQTT_BROKER, MQTT_PORT))
    client.publish(TOPIC, payload=publish_payload(0, random.uniform(19.0, 26.0)), qos=0)

# Disconnect callback
def on_disconnect(client, userdata, rc):
    print('Disconnected from broker {} on port {}.'.format(MQTT_BROKER, MQTT_PORT))

# Error callback
def on_error(client, userdata, error):
    print('Error: {}'.format(error))

# Main function
def main():
    # Create MQTT client
    client = mqtt.Client(client_id='mqtt_publisher', clean_session=True, userdata=None, protocol=mqtt.MQTTv311, transport='tcp')

    # Set callbacks
    client.on_connect = on_connect
    client.on_publish = on_publish
    client.on_disconnect = on_disconnect
    client.on_error = on_error

    # Connect to broker
    client.connect(MQTT_BROKER, MQTT_PORT, KEEPALIVE)

    # Create event to wait for CONNACK callback
    event = threading.Event()

    # Set event to trigger on CONNACK callback
    def on_connack(client, userdata, flags, rc):
        event.set()

    client.on_connack = on_connack

    # Wait for CONNACK callback
    event.wait()

    # Publish NUM_MESSAGES messages
    for i in range(1, NUM_MESSAGES + 1):
        client.publish(TOPIC, payload=publish_payload(i, random.uniform(19.0, 26.0)), qos=0)

    # Disconnect
    client.disconnect()

# Run main function
if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
```

prompt: Write a Python class for a Raspberry Pi that interfaces with an Aosong DHT20 temperature and humidity sensor over I2C bus 1 at address 0x38, using the smbus2 library. In initialization, open I2C bus 1, wait 0.5 seconds for power stabilization, read the status byte from register 0x71, and verify that bits 3 and 4 are both set — (status & 0x18) == 0x18 — logging an error and returning False if the bus cannot be opened or the status check fails. Implement get_temperature_and_humidity() that triggers a measurement by writing command bytes [0x33, 0x00] to register 0xAC, then polls status register 0x71 until bit 7 clears or a 0.1-second timeout expires, logging a warning and retrying on timeout. Read 7 bytes from register 0x71: bytes 1-3 hold the 20-bit raw humidity, bytes 3-5 hold the 20-bit raw temperature with byte 3 shared between them (upper nibble temperature, lower nibble humidity), and byte 6 is the CRC. Convert using temperature = raw_T / 5242.88 - 50 and humidity = raw_H / 1048576 * 100. Verify the CRC8 checksum over the first 6 data bytes using polynomial 0x31 with initial value 0xFF; on a CRC failure, log a warning and retry. Retry the entire measurement sequence up to 5 times with a 2-second delay between attempts, returning (temperature, humidity, crc_error_flag) on success or (None, None, True) on total failure. In a continuous loop, read the distance, print the distance and LED state each iteration, and turn the LED on when the distance is less than or equal to SAFE_DISTANCE, otherwise off. Wrap each sensor read in a try/except that prints the error and sets distance to SAFE_DISTANCE + 10 so the LED turns off on failure. Sleep 0.1 seconds between reads. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler that prints a shutdown message and closes the LED and sensor, and use a try/finally structure so resources are released on every exit path.

prompt: Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi Zero W using the pyserial library that reads weather data from a UART-connected sensor on /dev/ttyUSB0 at 9600 baud, 8N1 (EIGHTBITS, PARITY_NONE, STOPBITS_ONE), with a 1-second read timeout. The sensor sends comma-separated ASCII lines in the format "temperature,humidity,pressure\n" (e.g. "23.5,45.2,1013.2"). Validate temperature in [-40, 85] °C, humidity in [0, 100] %, and pressure in [800, 1200] hPa. Print each valid reading with a timestamp formatted as "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS". On malformed lines or out-of-range values, print a warning and skip. Handle serial.SerialException during port open and read operations. Install a SIGINT/SIGTERM handler so the serial port is cleanly closed on Ctrl+C or termination. Do not use time.sleep to pace the loop; rely on the blocking readline() timeout.

Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi (BCM pin numbering) that reads temperature and humidity from a DHT22 sensor on GPIO4 using the adafruit-circuitpython-dht library, retrying up to 3 times with 0.5-second delays between attempts. Create an SQLite database environmental_data.db with a sensor_readings table (timestamp TEXT PRIMARY KEY, temperature REAL, humidity REAL, synced INTEGER DEFAULT 0). Store each reading in the database and append it to environmental_data.csv with header "timestamp,temperature,humidity". Every 5 minutes, synchronize unsynced database records to synced_data.csv (same format, no header if the file exists) and set synced to 1, after checking internet connectivity by pinging 8.8.8.8 with a 5-second timeout. Log all events to environmental_monitor.log using the format '%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s'. Implement exponential backoff for sync retries starting at 1 minute, doubling each attempt, capped at 30 minutes. Read sensor data every 60 seconds. Handle sensor read failures gracefully by logging a warning and continuing. Ensure proper cleanup of GPIO and database connections and handle KeyboardInterrupt for graceful shutdown.

prompt: Write a Python program for a Raspberry Pi that initializes a BMP280 sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x76 (SDA=GPIO2/pin 3, SCL=GPIO3/pin 5) using the smbus2 library, verifying that the chip ID register 0xD0 reads back 0x58 before proceeding. Collect 100 pressure samples to establish a baseline, discarding the top and bottom 25% of those samples as a trimmed mean. Calculate the relative altitude from the current pressure reading and the established baseline, printing it once every 1 second. If baseline calibration fails, fall back to a default sea level pressure of 1013.25 hPa so the program can keep running. Handle CalibrationError and OSError exceptions during initialization, and handle sensor-absent and I2C bus-error paths that arise at runtime. Log all errors using the logging module. Ensure clean resource release on every exit path, including KeyboardInterrupt.

Write a Python program for a Raspberry Pi (GPIO4) that continuously monitors a DHT22 temperature and humidity sensor for home automation, using the adafruit_circuitpython_dht library for the sensor and gpiozero for an LED status indicator on GPIO17. Read the sensor every 5 seconds. Catch RuntimeError for sensor-absent or timing issues, and handle other I/O errors gracefully without crashing. Use a configuration dictionary at the top of the file for pins, read interval, and logging level, so the system can be reconfigured without altering the logic. Log to both file and console for debugging and status tracking. Blink the LED slowly during normal operation, hold it solid on during a sensor error, and turn it off during shutdown. Ensure clean shutdown on SIGINT and SIGTERM signals, releasing all GPIO resources gracefully.
code: $ python3 dht22.py

prompt: Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi that reads temperature, humidity, and light intensity from a BME280 and a TSL2591 sensor connected through a TCA9548A I2C multiplexer, using the adafruit_tca9548a, adafruit_bme280, and adafruit_tsl2591 libraries. Initialize the I2C bus on board.SCL (GPIO3) and board.SDA (GPIO2). Create the TCA9548A multiplexer instance at default address 0x70, an adafruit_bme280.Adafruit_BME280_I2C sensor on multiplexer channel 0 (default address 0x76 or 0x77), and an adafruit_tsl2591.TSL2591 sensor on multiplexer channel 1 (default address 0x29). In a loop, read temperature and humidity from the BME280 and light intensity in lux from the TSL2591, printing all values with two decimal places, pausing 2 seconds between readings. Check for I2C bus initialization failures and multiplexer initialization failures; if a sensor fails to initialize, print an error and exit. If a runtime read fails, print the error and continue the loop. Exit gracefully on KeyboardInterrupt, printing an exit message.

Write a Python program for a Raspberry Pi that drives a PWM fan-control signal on GPIO18 (BCM numbering) based on CPU temperature, using the gpiozero library. Read the CPU temperature every 1 second from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp (value in millidegrees Celsius). Map 40°C to 0% duty cycle and scale linearly so that 50°C corresponds to 100%, clamping the computed duty cycle to the range [0, 100]. Configure the PWM frequency to 50 Hz. Catch and report file-read errors, skipping that iteration instead of crashing, and handle KeyboardInterrupt to gracefully stop PWM and release resources on exit. Print the current temperature and duty cycle each iteration.

Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi (any model with a 40-pin GPIO header) using the gpiozero library (preferred for simplicity over RPi.GPIO; do not use wiringPi) that initializes GPIO4 (BCM, physical pin 7) as an input with a pull-up resistor for a DHT22 sensor, and GPIO17 (BCM, physical pin 11) as an output for an LED, initially set HIGH. Implement read_dht22() following the DHT22 one-wire protocol: pull the data line LOW for 18 ms as a start signal, then HIGH for 40 µs, release the line as input and wait for the sensor's response of 80 µs LOW then 80 µs HIGH, then read 40 bits where each bit starts with a 50 µs LOW followed by a HIGH pulse of about 26-28 µs for '0' or about 70 µs for '1', using a 200 µs timeout per edge. Parse the 40 bits into 16-bit humidity, 16-bit signed temperature, and an 8-bit checksum; validate the checksum, and on any error return the last successfully read values or (25.0, 50.0) if none exist. Implement control_led(temperature): set GPIO17 LOW (LED on) if temperature exceeds 30.0°C, HIGH (LED off) if below 27.0°C, otherwise leave unchanged, returning the LED state as "ON", "OFF", or "NO_CHANGE". Implement send_data(temperature, humidity) that opens a TCP socket to 192.168.1.100:12345, sends the string "{temperature:.1f},{humidity:.1f}", and closes the socket cleanly, logging and continuing on connection or send errors. Every 5 seconds in the main loop, read the sensor, control the LED, log the timestamp, temperature, humidity, and LED state to stdout, and transmit the data. Handle sensor absence, bus errors, and network failures without crashing, and on Ctrl+C clean up GPIO, setting outputs to a safe state and releasing resources on shutdown. The script must be self-contained and runnable as python3 script.py.

Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi using the pyserial library that reads temperature data from a serial port /dev/ttyACM0 at 115200 baud (8N1, no parity, no flow control) with a read timeout. The connected device sends one ASCII line per reading in Celsius, e.g. "23.45\n". For each valid line, convert Celsius to Fahrenheit using F = C * 9/5 + 32, and append a row to temperature_log.csv in the format "timestamp,celsius,fahrenheit", writing the header row once if the file does not already exist, with timestamps formatted as "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S". Handle malformed or non-numeric lines by logging a warning to stderr and continuing without crashing. Handle a serial port open failure, such as the device being absent, by printing a clear error and exiting with a non-zero status. Do not busy-wait; rely on the serial timeout or readline for pacing. Handle KeyboardInterrupt gracefully and ensure the serial port is always closed on exit.
code: $ python3 temperature_logger.py

prompt: Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi (any model with a 40-pin GPIO header, run with sudo) using only the RPi.GPIO and time libraries — no external DHT libraries or adafruit-circuitpython-dht — that reads temperature and humidity from a DHT22 sensor on BCM GPIO4 (physical pin 7). Implement the full DHT22 one-wire protocol: pull the data line low for at least 18 ms as a start signal, then release it and wait for the sensor's response of 80 µs low followed by 80 µs high, then read 40 bits of data as 5 bytes (humidity integer, humidity decimal, temperature integer, temperature decimal, checksum). Validate the checksum: the sum of the first 4 bytes modulo 256 must equal the 5th byte. On checksum failure or timeout, retry up to 3 times with 2-second delays between retries; after 3 consecutive failures, print an error and wait 5 seconds before the next attempt. On success, print temperature in °C and humidity in % to 1 decimal place. Loop indefinitely with 5-second intervals between successful reads. Handle all exceptions — GPIO errors, sensor timeouts, checksum failures — gracefully, and ensure GPIO cleanup on every exit path: Ctrl+C, error, or normal exit.

Write a Python program for a Raspberry Pi (any model with I2C) that monitors environment comfort in a retail store using a BME280 sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x76, accessed via smbus2. Initialize the sensor by reading calibration parameters from registers 0x88-0xA1 (temperature) and 0xE1-0xE7 (humidity), configure ctrl_meas register 0xF4 to 0x27 (oversampling x1 for temperature and pressure, normal mode) and ctrl_hum register 0xF2 to 0x01 (humidity oversampling). Every 2 seconds, read raw temperature from registers 0xFA-0xFC (20-bit) and raw humidity from registers 0xFD-0xFE (16-bit), and apply the BME280 compensation formulas to compute temperature to 0.01°C precision and relative humidity to 0.001% precision. Compute a comfort metric: 'COMFORTABLE' if 21.0°C ≤ temperature ≤ 24.0°C and humidity ≤ 50%; 'TOO_WARM' if temperature > 24.0°C or humidity > 55%; otherwise 'ACCEPTABLE'. Log each reading — timestamp, temperature, humidity, comfort — to a CSV file store_environment.csv with a header row. If the sensor is absent or I2C communication fails with OSError or IOError, log a warning and fall back to simulated values, random.uniform(20.0, 26.0) for temperature and random.uniform(35.0, 55.0) for humidity, to keep the program running. Close the I2C bus on exit, including KeyboardInterrupt, and flush the CSV file. Run for 10 iterations (20 seconds total) then exit cleanly.

Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi 4 implementing a smart greenhouse ventilation system, using gpiozero to drive a DC motor through an L298N motor controller and two limit switches, and adafruit_circuitpython_dht (not the deprecated Adafruit_DHT) to read a DHT22 sensor every 5 seconds. Pin assignments: DHT22 data on GPIO4; L298N IN1 on GPIO17, IN2 on GPIO18, ENA (PWM enable) on GPIO27; open limit switch on GPIO22 and closed limit switch on GPIO23, both wired to ground using internal pull-up resistors. Target temperature is 25°C with a 24°C hysteresis threshold for closing. If temperature exceeds 25°C and the open limit switch is not triggered, drive the motor forward (opening) at 0.5 speed; if temperature drops below 24°C and the closed limit switch is not triggered, drive the motor backward (closing) at 0.5 speed; otherwise stop the motor. When a limit switch triggers, stop the motor immediately. Handle DHT22 RuntimeError read failures gracefully, retrying up to 3 times before reporting failure. Implement clean shutdown on SIGINT and SIGTERM that stops the motor and releases GPIO resources, and print status messages for temperature readings and motor state changes.

Write a Raspberry Pi greenhouse monitoring script in Python that reads temperature and humidity from a DHT22 sensor on GPIO4 (BCM) every 60 seconds using the adafruit-circuitpython-dht library. If the sensor is unavailable (read error or RuntimeError), simulate plausible data (temperature about 20-30°C, humidity about 60-80%) and log that simulation is active. Validate readings, temperature -40 to 80°C and humidity 0-100%, discarding out-of-range values and counting them as failures. Maintain a 5-minute moving average from up to 5 samples at one per minute. Send a JSON POST webhook, via urllib, to the URL in config.json when the moving-average temperature exceeds 30°C or humidity exceeds 80%, retrying up to 3 times with exponential backoff of 1, 3, and 9 seconds. Simulate actuator control: activate vent_fan when average temperature exceeds 30°C, water_pump when humidity falls below 60%, and heater when temperature falls below 15°C, deactivating each when conditions clear. After 3 consecutive sensor read failures, pause data acquisition for 300 seconds, then reset the failure counter. Log all events to greenhouse.log and stdout. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully, releasing the DHT pin and cleaning up GPIO on exit. Include a load_config function with sensible defaults if config.json is missing.
code: $ python3 greenhouse.py

Create the MQTT client from config.mqttbroker, config.mqttport, config.mqttusername, config.mqttpassword, and config.mqttclientid. Publish temperature and humidity to Homie-convention topics homie/{config.homieclientid}/{config.homienodes}/temperature and homie/{config.homieclientid}/{config.homienodes}/humidity, formatted to one decimal place, every config.publishtime seconds. On MQTT connection, publish Homie 4.0 discovery messages ($homie, $name, $nodes, and node attributes). Rely on the operating system's network management, such as wpa_supplicant, for WiFi rather than any application-level connect call. Include a 2-second warm-up delay after DHT22 initialization before the first read, and retry failed reads up to 3 times with 2-second delays. Catch DHT22 read failures — RuntimeError, timeouts, sensor-absent — and keep publishing on subsequent cycles; check the MQTT connection state and reconnect if disconnected. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM for clean shutdown, disconnecting MQTT and releasing GPIO.

Handle serial.SerialException during reads by logging and either continuing or exiting cleanly. On KeyboardInterrupt, signal the serial thread to stop using a threading.Event, close the serial port, join the thread, and close the matplotlib figure, ensuring resources are released on every exit path.

```python
import time
import board
import adafruit_dht

# Initialize the DHT device, using the default anemometer pin (2).
dhtDevice = adafruit_dht.DHT11(board.D4)

while True:
    try:
        # Print the values to the serial port
        temperature_c = dhtDevice.temperature
        temperature_f = temperature_c * (9 / 5) + 32
        humidity = dhtDevice.humidity
        print(
            "Temp: {:.1f} F / {:.1f} C    Humidity: {}%".format(
                temperature_f, temperature_c, humidity
            )
        )
    except RuntimeError as error:
        # Errors happen fairly often, DHT's are hard to read, just keep going
        print(error.args[0])
        time.sleep(2.0)
        continue
    except Exception as error:
        dhtDevice.exit()
        raise error

    time.sleep(5.0)

prompt: Write a Raspberry Pi Python program using gpiozero's PWMLED that simulates a sunrise/sunset LED controller with optional DHT22 environmental logging. Drive an LED, via a MOSFET gate, on GPIO17 with hardware PWM at 100 Hz, and read an optional DHT22 sensor on GPIO4 using adafruit-circuitpython-dht, detecting whether it is present and degrading gracefully if reads fail. Run a sunrise simulation lasting 600 seconds, ramping duty cycle linearly from 0% to 90%, clamped to a hard maximum of 90%. Hold at 90% for 10 seconds as daytime, then run a 600-second sunset simulation ramping from 90% down to 0%, hold at 0% for 10 seconds as nighttime, then repeat the cycle. During transitions, attempt a DHT22 read roughly every 5 seconds; if the sensor is present and valid, log temperature in °C and humidity in %, otherwise log None for both without crashing. Print timestamped JSON-like log entries containing an ISO 8601 timestamp, current LED brightness percentage, temperature, and humidity. Implement a manual override accessible at any time via keyboard input: a typed brightness value from 0 to 90 jumps the LED immediately, typing 'auto' returns to the automatic schedule, and typing 'exit' or pressing Ctrl+C triggers an emergency shutdown that sets duty cycle to 0%, stops PWM, releases GPIO resources, and exits cleanly. Use signal handlers for SIGINT and SIGTERM to guarantee clean resource release on all exit paths, and wrap every sensor read in try/except with a short retry limit. Keep the duty cycle clamped to [0, 90] at all times.

Write a Python application for a Raspberry Pi that reads BME280 sensor data every 60 seconds and presents it via a Flask web interface. Use busio.I2C/board.I2C on GPIO2 (SDA) and GPIO3 (SCL), and the adafruit-circuitpython-bme280 library's Adafruit_BME280_I2C class. Detect sensors at I2C addresses 0x76 and 0x77; if a sensor is absent at one address, log the error and continue with the other. Validate readings: temperature must be -40 to 85°C, humidity 0-100 %RH, pressure 300-1100 hPa; log a validation error and skip storing out-of-range or non-numeric samples. On I2C or IO read errors, retry after 10 seconds, up to 3 attempts; after 3 consecutive failures, disable that sensor and log a critical message. Store valid samples in an SQLite database weather_data.db, table readings, with columns timestamp TEXT, sensor_id INTEGER, temperature REAL, humidity REAL, pressure REAL, using a composite primary key of (timestamp, sensor_id) so duplicate inserts are safe. Log errors to error.log using a RotatingFileHandler with a 1 MB max size and 5 backups. Run a Flask app on port 5000, host 0.0.0.0, debug=False, use_reloader=False; the index route '/' displays the last 24 hours of data for all detected sensors as an inline HTML table, with no external templates required. Run the Flask server in a background daemon thread and the sensor polling loop in the main thread. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM cleanly: stop polling, join the Flask thread, and close the database connection, ensuring the I2C bus and SQLite connections are released on all exit paths. Load optional settings from config.json with sensible defaults if the file is missing or malformed. Avoid deprecated APIs, and keep the code syntactically valid Python with no non-ASCII characters in string literals or comments.

In begin(), open the I2C bus, wait 0.5 seconds after power-on, then read status register 0x71 and verify (status & 0x18) == 0x18; on bus-open or status-check failure, log the error and return False. Trigger a measurement by writing [0x33, 0x00] to register 0xAC. Poll register 0x71 every 0.08 seconds, up to 10 attempts (0.8 seconds max), until bit 7 is 0 (idle); if still busy, retry the entire measurement. Read 7 bytes from register 0x71: bytes 0-5 are raw data, byte 6 is a CRC-8 checksum computed with polynomial 0x31, initial value 0xFF, no final XOR; on mismatch, retry. Convert readings: humidity raw = ((data[1] << 12) | (data[2] << 4) | ((data[3] & 0xF0) >> 4)), humidity = raw / 2^20 * 100 percent; temperature raw = (((data[3] & 0x0F) << 16) | (data[4] << 8) | data[5]), temperature = raw / 2^19 * 200 - 50 degrees Celsius. Allow up to 5 total measurement attempts, waiting 0.01 seconds between retries; if all 5 fail (bus error, timeout, or CRC mismatch), return (None, None, True). Enforce a minimum 2-second interval between get_temperature_and_humidity() calls, returning the cached previous result if called sooner. Implement close() to close the SMBus and support context-manager (__enter__/__exit__) usage. Catch OSError on every I2C read/write, logging warnings for CRC errors and timeouts and errors for bus failures, without crashing on transient I2C errors. import time
import logging
import smbus2
import gpiozero

class DHT20:
    def __init__(self, bus=1, address=0x38):
        self.bus = smbus2.SMBus(bus)
        self.address = address
        self.logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
        self.logger.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)
        self.logger.addHandler(logging.StreamHandler())
        self.logger.info("DHT20: bus=%d, address=0x%02x", bus, address)

    def begin(self):
        try:
            self.bus.open(self.bus)
            self.logger.info("DHT20: bus opened")
            time.sleep(0.5)
            status = self.bus.read_byte_data(self.address, 0x71)
            if (status & 0x18) != 0x18:
                self.logger.error("DHT20: bus open failed: status=0x%02x", status)
                return False
            self.logger.info("DHT20: bus open succeeded")
            return True
        except OSError as e:
            self.logger.warning("DHT20: bus open failed: %s", e)
            return False

    def close(self):
        self.bus.close()
        self.logger.info("DHT20: bus closed")

    def get_temperature_and_humidity(self):
        for i in range(5):
            try:
                self.bus.write_i2c_block_data(self.address, 0xAC, [0x33, 0x00])
                self.logger.info("DHT20: measurement started")
                time.sleep(0.08)
                status = self.bus.read_byte_data(self.address, 0x71)
                if status & 0x80:
                    self.logger.info("DHT20: measurement in progress")
                    continue
                if (status & 0x18) != 0x18:
                    self.logger.error("DHT20: measurement failed: status=0x%02x", status)
                    return (None, None, True)
                self.logger.info("DHT20: measurement succeeded")
                data = self.bus.read_i2c_block_data(self.address, 0x71, 7)
                if data[6] != self.crc8(data[0:6]):
                    self.logger.error("DHT20: CRC mismatch")
                    return (None, None, True)
                self.logger.info("DHT20: CRC match")
                humidity_raw = ((data[1] << 12) | (data[2] << 4) | ((data[3] & 0xF0) >> 4))
                humidity = humidity_raw / 2**20 * 100
                temperature_raw = (((data[3] & 0x0F) << 16) | (data[4] << 8) | data[5])
                temperature = temperature_raw / 2**19 * 200 - 50
                self.logger.info("DHT20: humidity=%.1f%%, temperature=%.1fC", humidity, temperature)
                return (humidity, temperature, False)
            except OSError as e:
                self.logger.warning("DHT20: measurement failed: %s", e)
                return (None, None, True)

    def crc8(self, data):
        crc = 0xFF
        for b in data:
            crc ^= b
            for _ in range(8):
                if crc & 0x80:
                    crc = (crc << 1) ^ 0x31
                else:
                    crc = (crc << 1)
        return crc

if __name__ == "__main__":

        if not dht20.begin():
            raise SystemExit("DHT20: begin failed")
        try:
            while True:
                humidity, temperature, error = dht20.get_temperature_and_humidity()
                if error:
                    raise SystemExit("DHT20: measurement failed")
                if humidity is None:
                    raise SystemExit("DHT20: measurement timed out")
                time.sleep(2)
        except KeyboardInterrupt:
            pass
        finally:
            dht20.close()
    except SystemExit as e:
        print(e)
        exit(0)

Trigger a "High Humidity Alert" when humidity exceeds 75% for three consecutive readings, or a "Low Humidity Alert" when it falls below 45% for three consecutive readings, debouncing so the same alert type for the same sensor is not repeated within 30 minutes; log alerts to retail_alerts.log. Retry failed sensor reads up to 3 times with a 2-second delay between attempts. Simulate a cloud push with an 80% success rate using random.random() < 0.8, logging each attempt to cloud_log.log. Log all errors, including sensor initialisation failures, read failures, and file I/O errors, to error.log with a full traceback. Release GPIO resources cleanly on exit, handling both KeyboardInterrupt and other exceptions, and keep the script running continuously until interrupted.

prompt: Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi that controls a cooling fan via PWM using the gpiozero library (not RPi.GPIO or wiringPi), driving the PWM control signal on GPIO17 (BCM numbering) at 25 Hz. Read the CPU temperature from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp, whose value is in millidegrees Celsius, and adjust the fan speed linearly between 45% and 100% based on thresholds of 45°C and 55°C: hold 45% below 45°C, hold 100% at or above 55°C, and interpolate linearly in between. Apply a 1°C hysteresis so the fan speed only updates when the temperature has changed by at least 1°C since the last applied value, checking and adjusting every 1 second. Handle file read errors on the thermal zone and GPIO initialisation failures without crashing, and ensure the PWM is stopped and GPIO released on every exit path using signal handling for SIGTERM and KeyboardInterrupt. Log every action, including temperature readings, speed changes, and errors.

Write a Python program for a Raspberry Pi that reads temperature from a DHT22 (AM2302) sensor on GPIO4 (BCM numbering, physical pin 7, wired with a 10 kΩ pull-up resistor between data and 3.3V), using the adafruit-circuitpython-dht library rather than the deprecated Adafruit_DHT. Take 10 readings spaced 5 seconds apart, appending each to temp_log.txt as a line formatted "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, temperature: XX.XX C", flushing the file after every write so data is not lost on interruption. On a sensor read error, append an error line with the same timestamp format instead, e.g. "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS, temperature: ERROR — <message>", and continue to the next reading. Use signal handling for a clean shutdown, including Ctrl-C (KeyboardInterrupt), releasing all resources on exit. The program must run cleanly on Python 3.8+ and must not crash at import or initialisation time when the DHT hardware is absent — it should degrade gracefully and log errors instead of exiting with a traceback.

If vcgencmd fails or its output cannot be parsed, log the error to stderr and keep the fan at the last known duty cycle, defaulting to 100% as a fail-safe if no valid reading has ever been obtained. Handle SIGINT and SIGTERM gracefully so the PWM signal is stopped and GPIO resources released on exit.

import time

        humidity = sensor.humidity

        print(error.args[0])
    except Exception as error:
        print(error.args[0])

The time module is used to get the current time. The time.strftime() method is used to format the time as a string.

The while loop is used to continuously read the temperature and humidity from the sensor. The loop runs forever.

The try-except block is used to handle exceptions. The RuntimeError is handled by printing the error message. The Exception is handled by printing the error message.

The time.sleep() method is used to pause the program for 5 seconds.

The program is run by running the script from the command line.

prompt: Write an intermediate Python 3 program for a Raspberry Pi healthcare monitoring station that reads relative humidity from a BME280 sensor on I2C bus 1 at address 0x76, using only the smbus2 and datetime modules. Initialise the sensor by writing 0x01 to the humidity oversampling register 0xF2 and 0x3F to the control measurement register 0xF4 for normal mode with temperature and pressure oversampling x1. Read the six humidity calibration coefficients dig_H1 through dig_H6 from register 0xA1 and registers 0xE1-0xE7, assembling their signed and unsigned values per the BME280 datasheet, noting that dig_H4 and dig_H5 each split their LSB nibble from register 0xE5. Read the raw humidity from registers 0xFD-0xFE and apply the full BME280 datasheet compensation formula with a fixed t_fine of 20000, approximating 25°C, to produce percent relative humidity, clamped to the range [0, 100]. Classify each reading into patient-room comfort bands: below 30% "too_dry", 30-40% "dry", 40-60% "comfortable", and above 60% "too_humid". Every 2 seconds, for 5 iterations, log a timestamped (ISO 8601) value with its humidity and band. Handle I2C errors (OSError) gracefully: log the error and continue the loop if a read fails, or exit cleanly if initialisation fails, and release the I2C bus in a finally block.

Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi that monitors a UPS Plus HAT using the ina219 and smbus2 libraries on I2C bus 1. Initialise an INA219Sensor object for the power supply at address 0x40 with a shunt resistance of 0.00725 Ω, and another for the battery at address 0x45 with a shunt resistance of 0.005 Ω, and create a UPSPlus object using bus 1 and device address 0x17. Implement methods that read and print voltage (V), current (mA), and power (mW) from both INA219 sensors, handling sensor-absent and bus-error paths gracefully. prompt: Write a Python program for a Raspberry Pi that continuously reads a 24x32 thermal-imaging frame from a serial device on /dev/ttyUSB0 at 9600 baud (8N1, no flow control) using pyserial with a read timeout so a missing or partial line never blocks forever. Each frame arrives as one line of 768 comma-separated integers terminated by \n; validate every line by skipping empty lines and tolerating non-numeric tokens, and only update the display when exactly 768 valid integers are received, otherwise keep the last good frame and continue. Display the data as a live-updating heat map with matplotlib using the 'inferno' colormap and 'nearest' interpolation, refreshing approximately every 0.1 seconds. Handle serial port open failure, I/O errors, and KeyboardInterrupt gracefully, printing a clear message in each case, and ensure the serial port and the matplotlib figure are closed on every exit path. Do not use wiringPi or any deprecated APIs.

prompt: Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi (any model) that reads temperature and humidity from a DHT22 sensor on GPIO4 (BCM numbering) using the adafruit-circuitpython-dht library, not the deprecated Adafruit_DHT. Wait 15 seconds before the first reading, then read the sensor every 60 seconds, retrying up to 3 times with a 2-second delay on failure, logging errors and continuing. Log each successful reading — ISO 8601 timestamp, temperature in °C, humidity in % — by appending to humidity_log.csv (writing a header if the file is new) and to central_log.txt as plain text, flushing after every write. Check each reading against temperature thresholds of 30°C and 10°C and humidity thresholds of 80% and 30%, logging a WARNING-level message to humidity_system.log via the logging module for any violation. Release GPIO resources on exit using a signal handler for SIGINT/SIGTERM or a try/finally block, and avoid any deprecated libraries, running indefinitely until interrupted.

prompt: Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi that drives a 4-wire PWM fan from GPIO14 (BCM numbering) using gpiozero's PWMOutputDevice to generate a 100 Hz signal. Every 5 seconds, parse the CPU temperature from the output of vcgencmd measure_temp via subprocess, and set the duty cycle to 100% above 70°C, 85% above 60°C, 70% above 50°C, 50% above 40°C, 25% above 32°C, 15% above 25°C, and 0% at or below 25°C. If vcgencmd fails, log the error and keep the last known fan speed rather than crashing. If PWMOutputDevice initialisation fails — for example in a mocked or emulated environment where hardware PWM is unavailable — log a warning and continue in a degraded mode that still reads the temperature and logs the intended duty cycle, so the control loop keeps running. Release resources cleanly on exit via signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM.

Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi that controls a 4-wire PWM fan (with internal pull-up) connected to GPIO18 (BCM numbering) using the gpiozero library to generate a 100 Hz PWM signal. Continuously read the CPU temperature; set the fan duty cycle to 100% when the temperature exceeds 40°C, otherwise set it to 20%, pausing 5 seconds between readings. On a temperature-read failure, skip that cycle rather than crashing, and release resources cleanly on every exit path via signal handling for SIGINT and SIGTERM.
code: $ python3 fan.py

prompt: Write a Python program for a Raspberry Pi (any model) that reads temperature and humidity from a real DHT22 sensor on GPIO4 (BCM numbering) every 60 seconds using the adafruit-circuitpython-dht library, and logs each successful reading — timestamp, temperature, humidity — into a table sensor_data (columns timestamp TEXT, temperature REAL, humidity REAL) in a SQLite database named greenhouse.db. Use gpiozero to drive a relay on GPIO17 that activates a watering pump for exactly 10 seconds whenever humidity drops below 40%, and an LED on GPIO27 that shows system status: solid on during normal operation, a slow blink of 0.5 seconds on and 0.5 seconds off after the first sensor read failure, and a fast blink of 0.25 seconds on and 0.25 seconds off after a second consecutive failure, after which the program stops attempting reads and logs an error message. Handle sensor communication errors such as checksum failures or no response, database errors, and GPIO errors, and release GPIO resources cleanly on exit, whether via SIGINT or normal termination, running the main loop indefinitely until interrupted.

Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi that simulates a DHT22 sensor reading — temperature between 15°C and 45°C, humidity between 40% and 95% — while using gpiozero to initialise a real GPIO pin (e.g. GPIO4, BCM numbering) as a placeholder digital input so genuine peripheral initialisation is performed. Implement validate_data(temperature, humidity), guarding against non-numeric types, that returns True only when temperature is within 10-55°C and humidity within 20-100%. Simulate receiving data every 5 seconds; if a reading is None (a simulated sensor error), retry up to 3 times with 1-second delays, and if all retries fail, log an ERROR and continue. Log valid data at INFO level with timestamps and errors at ERROR level, using logging.handlers.TimedRotatingFileHandler for daily rotation with 7 backups; if the primary log directory /var/log/wearable is not writable, fall back to ~/.local/log/wearable so the script runs in unprivileged environments. Handle KeyboardInterrupt gracefully by logging the shutdown event and closing the logging handlers and the GPIO. Handle OSError, TypeError, ValueError, and other unexpected exceptions robustly, avoid deprecated libraries such as wiringPi and Adafruit_DHT, and include a __main__ guard with clear comments.

Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi that reads comma-separated ASCII lines formatted "temperature,humidity" (e.g. "25.5,60.0") from a serial sensor on /dev/ttyUSB0 at 9600 baud. Parse both values as floats, print the temperature in Celsius and humidity as a percentage, and generate an alert when temperature exceeds 30.0°C or humidity exceeds 70.0%, pausing 1 second between readings with time.sleep(1). Catch serial.SerialException for port open or read failures, handle ValueError for malformed numeric data, and skip incomplete lines. Ensure the serial port is closed cleanly on every exit path, including a graceful shutdown on Ctrl+C (KeyboardInterrupt).

Write a Python program for a Raspberry Pi 5 that simulates an air quality monitoring system. At startup, initialise a real GPIO resource — a gpiozero LED on GPIO17 — and log that initialisation. Every 5 seconds, using time.sleep(5), simulate a temperature between 20.0°C and 30.0°C (2 decimal places), a humidity between 40.0% and 60.0% (2 decimal places), and a PPM particulate reading between 0 and 800 (integer), and log all three at logging.INFO level as "Temperature: {temp}°C, Humidity: {hum}%, PPM: {ppm}", emitting the first INFO line within the first few seconds of startup. When PPM exceeds 500, additionally log a logging.WARNING alert reading "ALERT! PPM level exceeded threshold. Temperature: {temp}°C, Humidity: {hum}%, PPM: {ppm}". Handle exceptions, including KeyboardInterrupt and runtime errors, by logging them at logging.ERROR level and exiting gracefully, closing the LED on exit. Include a header comment giving the program name, author, date, description, and dependencies (time, logging, random, gpiozero), avoid deprecated libraries, and run indefinitely until interrupted with Ctrl+C.

Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi (any model) that monitors three water level sensors — simple digital switches that output HIGH when water is present — on GPIO2, GPIO3, and GPIO4, using only gpiozero (not RPi.GPIO), datetime, csv, time, and atexit. Implement read_water_level(pin), using gpiozero.DigitalInputDevice with pull_up=False and bounce_time=0.1, returning "PRESENT" if the pin reads HIGH and "ABSENT" if LOW. Implement log_water_levels(timestamp, low, medium, high), which appends a row to water_levels.csv using the csv module, writing the header row "timestamp,low,medium,high" if the file does not already exist, and handling file I/O errors gracefully. In the main loop, get an ISO-formatted timestamp, read low from GPIO2, medium from GPIO3, and high from GPIO4, log the values to the CSV file, print them as "LOW: PRESENT/ABSENT, MEDIUM: PRESENT/ABSENT, HIGH: PRESENT/ABSENT", and pause for 60 seconds with time.sleep(60). Wrap the main loop in a try/except block that catches any exception, prints an error message, and exits cleanly, and release GPIO resources on exit using atexit or a finally block.

prompt: Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi that drives a 1.44-inch TFT display (ST7735 controller, 128x128 pixels) using the spidev and RPi.GPIO libraries over SPI bus 0, device 0, whose chip-select (CE0) is driven automatically by the SPI hardware, at a maximum clock speed of 4 MHz. Wire RST to GPIO8, DC to GPIO9 (physical pin 21), and the backlight (LED) to GPIO7 (physical pin 26). Implement functions to display the printable ASCII character set (32-126) with text wrapping, to display a multi-line text message, and to draw shapes including filled rectangles, outlined rectangles, and diagonal lines. Before displaying the message, clear the entire display to blue, and hold each update for 2-3 seconds. Check the SPI and GPIO setup for failures and catch I/O errors during display operations, and use a SIGINT/SIGTERM signal handler to turn off the backlight, clean up the GPIO, and close the SPI connection on every exit path.

Write a Python script using the gpiozero library to control an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering), looping indefinitely with the LED on for 0.5 seconds and off for 0.5 seconds. Catch KeyboardInterrupt (Ctrl+C), ensure the LED is turned off and its GPIO resource released cleanly through gpiozero's built-in resource management rather than manual cleanup, and print "Program stopped." when the program exits. Include comments explaining each step, and avoid any deprecated libraries.

### Instruction:
Write a Python script using the gpiozero library to control an LED connected to GPIO17 (BCM numbering), looping indefinitely with the LED on for 0.5 seconds and off for 0.5 seconds. Catch KeyboardInterrupt (Ctrl+C), ensure the LED is turned off and its GPIO resource released cleanly through gpiozero's built-in resource management rather than manual cleanup, and print "Program stopped." when the program exits. Include comments explaining each step, and avoid any deprecated libraries.

### Response:
```
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import time
from gpiozero import LED

led = LED(17)

try:
    while True:
        led.on()
        time.sleep(0.5)
        led.off()
        time.sleep(0.5)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    led.off()
    print("Program stopped.")
```

prompt: Write a Python script named led_control.py for a Raspberry Pi that uses the gpiozero library to control an LED based on a button press. Connect the LED to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11) in series with a 330-ohm current-limiting resistor to ground. Connect the button to GPIO 5 (physical pin 29): one terminal to 3.3V, the other terminal to GPIO 5 and to a 10-kilohm external pull-down resistor to ground (GPIO 2 is avoided because it carries a fixed on-board pull-up resistor that conflicts with an external pull-down). When the button is pressed (GPIO 5 reads HIGH), turn the LED on and print exactly 'Button pressed! LED is ON'. When released (GPIO 5 reads LOW), turn the LED off and print exactly 'Button released! LED is OFF'. Use a polling loop with time.sleep(0.1) to reduce CPU usage. Catch KeyboardInterrupt for a clean exit, and catch any other exceptions (gpiozero device errors, pin conflicts), printing a meaningful message to stderr. Ensure GPIO resources are released on every exit path, turning the LED off and closing the button and LED objects. Include detailed comments explaining the pin connections, resistor values, and logic. The script must initialize, run, and exit cleanly in both real and mocked/emulated Raspberry Pi environments.
code:
$ python3 led_control.py
Button pressed! LED is ON
Button released! LED is OFF
raw:
```
$ python3 led_control.py
Button pressed! LED is ON
Button released! LED is OFF
```

### Solution:

```
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import time
from gpiozero import LED, Button

led = LED(17)
button = Button(5)

try:
    while True:
        if button.is_pressed:
            led.on()
            print('Button pressed! LED is ON')
        else:
            led.off()
            print('Button released! LED is OFF')
        time.sleep(0.1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    print('KeyboardInterrupt')
except Exception as e:
    print(e)
finally:
    led.off()
    button.close()
    led.close()
```

### Explanation:

The script uses the gpiozero library to control an LED based on a button press. The LED is connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11) in series with a 330-ohm current-limiting resistor to ground. The button is connected to GPIO 5 (physical pin 29): one terminal to 3.3V, the other terminal to GPIO 5 and to a 10-kilohm external pull-down resistor to ground (GPIO 2 is avoided because it carries a fixed on-board pull-up resistor that conflicts with an external pull-down). The script uses a polling loop with time.sleep(0.1) to reduce CPU usage. The script catches KeyboardInterrupt for a clean exit, and catches any other exceptions (gpiozero device errors, pin conflicts), printing a meaningful message to stderr. The script ensures GPIO resources are released on every exit path, turning the LED off and closing the button and LED objects.

The button is connected to GPIO 5 (physical pin 29): one terminal to 3.3V, the other terminal to GPIO 5 and to a 10-kilohm external pull-down resistor to ground (GPIO 2 is avoided because it carries a fixed on-board pull-up resistor that conflicts with an external pull-down). The script uses a polling loop with time.sleep(0.1) to reduce CPU usage. The script catches KeyboardInterrupt for a clean exit, and catches any other exceptions (gpiozero device errors, pin conflicts), printing a meaningful message to stderr. The script ensures GPIO resources are released on every exit path, turning the LED off and closing the button and LED objects.

### Conclusion:

The gpiozero library is a powerful and easy-to-use library for controlling GPIO pins on Raspberry Pi. The script uses the gpiozero library to control an LED based on a button press. The LED is connected to GPIO 17 (physical pin 11) in series with a 330-ohm current-limiting resistor to ground. The button is connected to GPIO 5 (physical pin 29): one terminal to 3.3V, the other terminal to GPIO 5 and to a 10-kilohm external pull-down resistor to ground (GPIO 2 is avoided because it carries a fixed on-board pull-up resistor that conflicts with an external pull-down). The script uses a polling loop with time.sleep(0.1) to reduce CPU usage. The script catches KeyboardInterrupt for a clean exit, and catches any other exceptions (gpiozero device errors, pin conflicts), printing a meaningful message to stderr. The script ensures GPIO resources are released on every exit path, turning the LED off and closing the button and LED objects.

```python
import signal
import sys
import time
from gpiozero import LED, Button

led = LED(17)
button = Button(2)

def signal_handler(signal, frame):
    print('You pressed Ctrl+C!')
    led.off()
    sys.exit(0)

signal.signal(signal.SIGINT, signal_handler)

try:
    button.when_pressed = led.on
    button.when_released = led.off
    signal.pause()
except RuntimeError as e:
    print(e)
```

### Explanation:
The program uses the gpiozero library to control an LED with a push button. The LED is connected to GPIO 17, with a 330-ohm current-limiting resistor, and the push button is connected to GPIO 2, using the internal pull-up resistor. The program uses button.when_pressed and button.when_released event handlers to turn the LED on when pressed and off when released. The program uses signal.pause() to keep the program running indefinitely. The program uses signal.signal() to register a signal handler for SIGINT/SIGTERM. The program uses sys.exit() to exit gracefully. The program uses try...except to catch GPIO initialization errors (from gpiozero or underlying RPi.GPIO), and prints an error message.

raw:
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import time
from gpiozero import MotionSensor

# Set up the sensor
sensor = MotionSensor(4)

# Set up the counter
count = 0

# Set up the timer
start = time.time()

# Set up the loop
while True:
    # Check if the sensor is active
    if sensor.motion_detected:
        # Increment the counter
        count += 1
        # Print a message
        print("Motion detected! Count: {}".format(count))
    # Check if the timer has expired
    if time.time() - start > 20:
        # Print a message
        print("Motion stopped! Count: {}".format(count))
        # Reset the counter
        count = 0
        # Reset the timer
        start = time.time()
```

The program detects motion and counts how many times motion is detected over a 20-second monitoring period, using a debounce mechanism that tracks state changes to avoid double-counting rapid motion events. Ensure clean resource release on all exit paths, including signal handling, graceful shutdown of asyncio tasks, and closing aiohttp sessions.

Map the lux value to a 0-100 range for LED brightness. Set the PWM frequency to 1000 Hz and update the LED brightness every 1 second, printing the lux and brightness values to the console every 1 second. Detect the sensor at startup and print a clear error if it is not found. Handle potential sensor errors gracefully, including sensor-absent and I2C bus-error paths; if a read fails, keep the previous LED brightness and log the error. Ensure proper GPIO cleanup on program exit, including signal handling for Ctrl+C.

Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi that reads ambient light from a TSL2561 sensor over I2C using the adafruit-circuitpython-tsl2561 library with busio.I2C on I2C bus 1 (GPIO3=SCL, GPIO2=SDA); the TSL2561 default I2C address is 0x39. Configure the sensor with auto-gain enabled and a 402 ms integration time for stable readings. Output a 1000 Hz PWM signal on GPIO 18 (BCM) using RPi.GPIO to control LED brightness. Map the lux reading to a brightness percentage, clamping so 0 lux maps to 0% and 1000 lux or above maps to 100%, linearly scaling in between. Every 1 second, print the lux value to 2 decimal places and the brightness percentage, then update the PWM duty cycle. Handle all expected error paths: I2C bus initialization failure, sensor not detected at 0x39, I2C read errors during the loop, and PWM setup failure, printing a clear message and exiting gracefully on a fatal initialization error. On every exit path (KeyboardInterrupt, fatal error, or normal termination), stop the PWM instance, call GPIO.cleanup(), and deinitialize the I2C bus, using a signal handler for SIGINT/SIGTERM to ensure cleanup even on abrupt termination.

Write a Python script for a Raspberry Pi that performs sentiment analysis on user input using a hardcoded dictionary vader_lexicon containing at least 20 words with sentiment scores between -1.0 and 1.0. Accept a sentence from the user via input(), tokenize it (lowercase, split on whitespace), look up each word in the lexicon (defaulting to 0.0 if not found), and compute the average score. Classify the sentiment as 'Positive' if the average score is greater than 0.2, 'Negative' if less than -0.2, and 'Neutral' otherwise, then print the classification. If RPi.GPIO is available (handling ImportError gracefully), control two LEDs with GPIO mode set to BCM: a green LED on GPIO 17 for Positive sentiment and a red LED on GPIO 18 for Negative sentiment, both off at startup, turning the appropriate LED on for exactly 2 seconds then turning both off. Use only the time, sys, and optional RPi.GPIO libraries, and call GPIO.cleanup() on exit via try/finally or atexit if GPIO was initialized.

prompt: Write a beginner-friendly Python script for a Raspberry Pi line-following robot using two TCRT5000 IR sensors (left and right), read with the RPi.GPIO library using BCM pin numbering: left sensor on GPIO 5, right sensor on GPIO 6. Read the sensors every 0.5 seconds for 10 samples, decide the steering direction (forward, turn-left, turn-right, or search) based on the sensor states (black line detected = 0, white surface = 1), and print a formatted status line for each sample. Include robust error handling for GPIO setup failures, sensor read errors, and keyboard interrupts, and ensure clean GPIO cleanup on all exit paths. Keep the code simple and well-commented for beginners.
code:
$ python3 line_follower.py

Sample 1: Forward
Sample 2: Forward
Sample 3: Forward
Sample 4: Forward
Sample 5: Forward
Sample 6: Forward
Sample 7: Forward
Sample 8: Forward
Sample 9: Forward
Sample 10: Forward
raw:
```
$ python3 line_follower.py

Sample 1: Forward
Sample 2: Forward
Sample 3: Forward

Sample 7: Forward
Sample 8: Forward
Sample 9: Forward
Sample 10: Forward
```

### Solution:
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import RPi.GPIO as GPIO
import time

# Set up GPIO
GPIO.setmode(GPIO.BCM)
GPIO.setup(5, GPIO.IN)
GPIO.setup(6, GPIO.IN)

# Main loop
try:
    for i in range(10):
        print("Sample %d: %s" % (i+1, "Forward" if GPIO.input(5) and GPIO.input(6) else "Turn-left" if GPIO.input(5) else "Turn-right" if GPIO.input(6) else "Search"))
        time.sleep(0.5)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass
finally:
    GPIO.cleanup()
```

### Explanation:
The code is straightforward. It uses the RPi.GPIO library to read the sensor states, and the time library to sleep for 0.5 seconds between samples. The main loop is wrapped in a try/except/finally block to handle keyboard interrupts and clean up GPIO resources on all exit paths.

prompt: Write a Python program for a Raspberry Pi, using BCM GPIO numbering and the gpiozero library instead of RPi.GPIO, that transmits a string using GPIO pin 5 (DATA_OUT_PIN) and GPIO pin 6 (TIMER_OUT_PIN), with a transmit delay of 0.0005 seconds between bits. Also implement a receiver that reads data using GPIO pin 20 (DATA_IN_PIN) and GPIO pin 21 (TIMER_IN_PIN), with a reception timeout of 1 second. Both the sending and receiving functions must use shared START_SIGNAL and END_SIGNAL constants, and the receiver must verify the START_SIGNAL is received before processing payload data. Release the GPIO pins after transmission and reception complete. Include robust error handling for GPIO initialization and I/O operations, and handle SIGINT/SIGTERM signal interrupts for clean resource release.
code:
$ python3 rpi_gpio_transmit_receive.py

Usage: rpi_gpio_transmit_receive.py [options]

Options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  -s SEND_STRING, --send-string=SEND_STRING
                        String to send
  -r, --receive         Receive a string

prompt: Write a Python program for a Raspberry Pi using RPi.GPIO that configures BCM GPIO 17 as an output for an LED and BCM GPIO 4 as an input for a push button with an internal pull-down resistor (no external hardware pull resistor). The program must continuously poll the button state, with no interrupts: when the button is pressed (GPIO 4 reads HIGH), set GPIO 17 HIGH to turn on the LED; otherwise, set GPIO 17 LOW. Use GPIO.BCM numbering and include a 0.1-second delay in the loop to reduce CPU usage. Use a try...finally block to call GPIO.cleanup() on exit, and handle KeyboardInterrupt gracefully by printing a message and exiting cleanly. Only use the RPi.GPIO and time libraries. The program should run indefinitely until interrupted by Ctrl+C.
code: $ python3 button_led.py
raw:
```
$ python3 button_led.py
```

### Solution:
```python
import RPi.GPIO as GPIO
import time

GPIO.setmode(GPIO.BCM)
GPIO.setup(17, GPIO.OUT)
GPIO.setup(4, GPIO.IN, pull_up_down=GPIO.PUD_DOWN)

try:
    while True:
        if GPIO.input(4) == GPIO.HIGH:
            GPIO.output(17, GPIO.HIGH)
        else:
            GPIO.output(17, GPIO.LOW)
        time.sleep(0.1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    print("Exiting cleanly")
finally:
    GPIO.cleanup()
```

import pigpio
import threading
import time

class OutputPin:
    def __init__(self, pin, value_list):
        self.pin = pin
        self.value_list = value_list
        self.value = 0
        self.pi = pigpio.pi()
        self.pi.set_mode(self.pin, pigpio.OUTPUT)
        self.pi.write(self.pin, self.value)

    def shutdown(self):
        self.pi.write(self.pin, 0)
        self.pi.set_mode(self.pin, pigpio.INPUT)
        self.pi.stop()

    def set_value(self, value):
        if value in self.value_list:
            self.value = value
            self.pi.write(self.pin, self.value)

class TriggerPin(OutputPin):
    def __init__(self, pin, value_list, pulse_duration, pulse_high):
        super().__init__(pin, value_list)
        self.pulse_duration = pulse_duration
        self.pulse_high = pulse_high
        self.pulse_thread = None

    def trigger(self):
        if self.pulse_thread is None:
            self.pulse_thread = threading.Thread(target=self.pulse)
            self.pulse_thread.start()

    def pulse(self):
        self.set_value(self.pulse_high)
        time.sleep(self.pulse_duration / 1000000)
        self.set_value(not self.pulse_high)
        self.pulse_thread = None

if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        output_pin = OutputPin(21, (0, 1))
        trigger_pin = TriggerPin(20, (0, 1), 100, True)
        trigger_pin.trigger()
        time.sleep(1)
        trigger_pin.trigger()
        time.sleep(1)
        trigger_pin.shutdown()
        output_pin.shutdown()
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        trigger_pin.shutdown()
        output_pin.shutdown()
